sentences.text: Archaeopteryx was roughly the size of a Eurasian magpie or a raven, featuring broad wings with rounded ends and a long tail relative to its body length.

Its wings bore well-developed, markedly asymmetrical flight feathers with vanes stabilized by a complex barb-barbule-barbicel arrangement similar to modern birds, while its tail also carried broad feathers.

A 2011 study used scanning electron microscopy to analyze a single isolated feather, and comparisons with 87 modern bird species led researchers to calculate a 95% likelihood that the analyzed feather was originally black.
A 2006 study found that Archaeopteryx's leg feathers formed up to 12% of its total airfoil.

A 2002 scenario suggests Archaeopteryx used glides punctuated with shallow downstrokes to escape predators, while a 2018 study reported its flight stroke cycle was closer to the grabbing motion of maniraptorans than modern birds.
The genus Archaeopteryx was named by Meyer in 1861, originally based on a single feather found that same year.
All known fossils of Archaeopteryx come from limestone deposits near Solnhofen, Germany.
The Unnumbered Specimen was originally classified as Compsognathus by the amateur collector Friedrich Müller before being recognized as Archaeopteryx.
The Schamhaupten Specimen is the only known specimen lacking preserved feathers and comes from the Painten Formation, making it somewhat older than other Archaeopteryx specimens.
The Mühlheim Specimen was initially considered a thirteenth Archaeopteryx but was reassigned to the distinct genus Alcmonavis upon its 2019 description.
A 2004 CT scan of the London specimen showed Archaeopteryx had a significantly larger brain than most dinosaurs, indicating it had the brain size necessary for flight.
Archaeopteryx is inferred to have had the ability to fly or glide, and it most likely hunted small prey by seizing it with its jaws or claws.

Most Archaeopteryx specimens likely drifted on their backs in the sea before becoming embedded in anoxic sediment, resulting in a characteristic death pose with the head, neck, and tail bent downward due to muscle relaxation and early decomposition.
A 2009 histological study showed that Archaeopteryx had a relatively slow growth rate compared to modern birds, and all known skeletons are believed to come from juvenile specimens.

Authors speculated that Archaeopteryx and the flightless kiwi had similar basal metabolic rates, and comparisons of scleral rings suggest it may have been a diurnal animal, similar to many modern birds.

In 1960, Swinton proposed placing Archaeopteryx lithographica on the official genera list, rendering alternative names like Griphosaurus and Griphornis invalid, though a 2007 review concluded that two distinct species, A. lithographica and A. siemensii, could be supported based on well-preserved specimens including the Thermopolis find.

In 2007, Phil Senter suggested that Jurapteryx, A. siemensii, and A. bavarica are junior synonyms of A. lithographica, arguing that their diagnostic features can be explained by ontogeny, while John Ostrom considered Archaeopteryx to be remarkably similar to the theropod family Dromaeosauridae.
It is debated whether all discovered remains of Archaeopteryx belong to a single species or genus.
Archaeopteryx lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 150 million years ago, with some estimates placing its range between 150 and 148 million years ago.
